🔻 THEY ARE NOT JUST PRESERVING ORGANS ANYMORE. THEY ARE REPAIRING THEM. AND THE TRANSPLANT INDUSTRY IS PANICKING.

For seventy years, transplant medicine has followed one rule: keep the organ alive until it reaches the patient.

Slow the decay. Minimize the damage. Hope for the best.

That rule just changed.

A team of researchers published something this week that describes something entirely new:

Instead of just preserving donor organs, they are now repairing them while they wait.

The method is called mitochondrial transplantation.

Here is how it works:

When an organ is removed from a donor, it is connected to a machine that keeps it alive outside the body. This is called machine perfusion. It has been used for years.

But now, instead of just pumping blood through the organ, doctors are injecting healthy mitochondria directly into it.

The results are striking.

In pig hearts, transplanted mitochondria improved contractile recovery and cut infarct size by more than 75%. In lungs, they improved oxygenation and reduced inflammation. In kidneys, they stimulated metabolic activity and energy production.

The mitochondria enter the cells. They replace damaged organelles. They restore energy production. They rebalance inflammatory signaling.

The authors described it as a shift from “preservation” to “repair.”

Think about that.

An organ that would have been discarded as too damaged for transplant can now be reconditioned. Repaired. Made viable again.

This is not science fiction. This is published in a peer-reviewed medical journal.

The MedBed community has always said that the body can heal itself if given the right tools.

Now they are giving organs the tools to heal themselves before they even reach the patient.

The line between “preservation” and “regeneration” just disappeared.

And the transplant industry knows it.

🇷🇺💥🇺🇦 Food Shortages Hit Ukraine as Russian Strikes Devastate Retail Logistics

Western media are now covering the impact of Russian strikes on food supply logistics in Ukraine. According to the Washington Post, Russia has shifted its strikes toward warehouses and distribution centers across the country, triggering shortages of fresh goods in grocery stores. The outlet reports that distribution centers belonging to Silpo and Novus were among those hit.

"Shelves have emptied out, with fresh produce and dairy products including sour cream, yogurt, and cheese disappearing. Some stores have filled empty space with surplus goods to minimize the visible sense of shortage. The government, seeking to avoid public panic, has issued no official warnings, though supermarkets have warned customers of temporary disruptions," the outlet writes.

The paper cites Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi, who says this won't lead to hunger or a systemic food shortage in Ukraine. "Roughly 90% of the food logistics serviced by retail chains has been destroyed, but that doesn't mean Ukrainians will be left without food. There's no threat of hunger or a systemic physical shortage of food," Vysotskyi said, according to the outlet.
